content: In certain species of diatoms, auxospores are specialized cells that are produced during critical stages of their cell cycle or life history. These cells play a significant role in processes such as growth, sexual reproduction, or dormancy. Auxospores are essential for restoring the normal size of diatom cells. This is because successive mitotic cell divisions result in a progressive reduction in cell size. During cell division, each daughter cell inherits one of the two silica valves that make up the cell wall and subsequently forms a smaller valve within it. As a result, the average size of diatom cells in a population decreases with each division cycle. When a diatom cell becomes too small, it produces an auxospore to expand its size back to the normal dimensions characteristic of vegetative cells. Auxospores also play a role in the sexual reproduction of diatoms. They may be formed after haploid gametes fuse to create a diploid zygote. Additionally, auxospores can serve as dormant stages, sometimes referred to as resting spores. These structures enable diatoms to survive during periods that are unfavorable for growth, such as during winter or when nutrients are depleted.
